facts.statement: Gigantornis eaglesomei was described from a fragmentary fossil found in the Eocene of Nigeria.
facts.quote: Gigantornis eaglesomei is a very large prehistoric bird described from a fragmentary specimen from the Eocene of Nigeria.

facts.statement: The only identified remains of Gigantornis consist of a broken sternum found in the Middle Eocene Ameki Formation at Ameki, Nigeria.
facts.quote: Its identified remains consist of a broken sternum found in Middle Eocene Ameki Formation deposits at Ameki (Nigeria).

facts.statement: Gigantornis was initially classified in the albatross family but is now placed in the pseudotooth bird family Pelagornithidae.
facts.quote: It was originally described as a representative of the albatross family, Diomedeidae, but was later referred to the pseudotooth or bony-toothed bird family, Pelagornithidae.

facts.statement: Gigantornis had an inferred wingspan of about 6 meters (20 feet), making it one of the largest birds ever.
facts.quote: Gigantornis is one of the largest pseudotooth birds, with an inferred wingspan of about 6 m (20 ft) it is among the largest birds ever.

facts.statement: The sternum of Gigantornis had a short and deep-crested shape typical of dynamic soarers.
facts.quote: The Gigantornis sternum is of the typical short and deep-crested shape found in dynamic soarers.

facts.statement: Gigantornis lived between 48.07 and 37.71 million years ago during the Lutetian to Bartonian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Lutetian to Bartonian (48.07 to 37.71 million years ago)

facts.statement: It is debated whether Gigantornis belongs to a distinct genus or is the same species as Dasornis emuinus.
facts.quote: It is not known whether this bird belongs to a distinct genus; it might even be the very same species as the similar-sized Dasornis emuinus

rejected.statement: The genus Gigantornis was originally described by Andrews in 1916.
